title: Hide Artifacts: Extended Attributes
summary: Extended Attributes describes hiding payloads inside the key and value metadata that macOS and Linux attach to files and directories. These attributes are not shown by ordinary tools such as Finder, ls or cat, and they persist because they are stored beside the file rather than inside its content. On Linux they are grouped into namespaces with different permission rules, and on macOS they appear as flat strings, many of them under the com.apple prefix and used by Gatekeeper and Spotlight. An adversary writes an encoded payload into an attribute of a legitimate file, then a small loader reads the attribute, decodes it and passes it to an interpreter. The file body and its hash stay the same, so content only integrity checks pass. Detection requires listing attributes, baselining them where they should not exist, and watching for commands that read attribute values in unusual contexts.

beginner.definition: Files carry more than their contents. They can also carry small labels called extended attributes, or xattrs for short. Each label is a pair made of a name and a value. Normal tools such as the file browser and the cat command do not show them. An attacker can hide a payload inside a label on a normal file.
beginner.whyItMatters: The file itself does not change, so its fingerprint stays the same. Many security checks compare file contents and see nothing wrong. The hidden payload appears only when you ask for the labels. This makes extended attributes a quiet hiding place. It also means that a clean scan is not proof that a file is safe.
howItWorks: Both macOS and Linux let a file store extra labels beside its normal contents.
Each label has a name and a value, and normal file viewers never display it.
Linux groups these labels into areas such as user and system, with different permission rules.
macOS uses flat label names, and many start with the com.apple prefix for system features.
An attacker writes an encoded payload into a label on a legitimate file.
A small loader reads the label, decodes it, and hands it to a script interpreter to run.
beginner.example: Imagine a suitcase at an airport. The suitcase looks the same as every other one, and the weight on the scale matches the ticket. A small tag is tied to the handle with a folded note inside it. Staff who check the size and the weight of the bag find nothing wrong. Only someone who unties the tag and opens the folded note reads the real message. Extended attributes are that tag. The bag is ordinary, but the important information travels beside it.
takeaways: Files can carry hidden labels that normal viewers never show you.
A matching file hash does not prove that no hidden data is attached.
Use the attribute listing tools on both Linux and macOS systems.

objectives: Explain what an extended attribute is and how it is stored next to a file.
Describe the difference between Linux attribute namespaces and macOS attribute names.
Explain how a payload can be stored in an attribute and later executed.
Identify the tools that list and read extended attribute values.
Explain why content only integrity checks can miss this hidden payload.
